title: Law of Equipartition of Energy
short_intro: The law of equipartition of energy states that in any dynamical system in thermal equilibrium, the total energy is shared equally among all active degrees of freedom. Each degree of freedom contributes an average thermal energy of (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T per molecule, or (1/2)RT per mole.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Calculation of degrees of freedom for monoatomic, diatomic, and triatomic gases; specific heat capacities (C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub>) and their ratio (γ).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Statistical derivation of the equipartition theorem using Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, vibrational modes of polyatomic gases at high temperatures, and deviations in specific heat at cryogenic temperatures.

concept_notes.heading: Statement of Equipartition of Energy
bullets: In thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature T, the average kinetic energy associated with each independent quadratic term in the generalized coordinates or velocities of a system is equal to (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T.
A degree of freedom represents an independent mode in which a molecule can store energy, typically corresponding to translational, rotational, or vibrational motions.
The theorem applies universally to classical systems where energy depends quadratically on position coordinates or momentum components.

concept_notes.heading: Degrees of Freedom (f) across Molecular Types
bullets: Monoatomic gases (e.g., He, Ar) possess 3 translational degrees of freedom: f = 3.
Rigid diatomic gases (e.g., O<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub> at room temperature) possess 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom: f = 5.
Non-rigid diatomic gases at high temperatures include an additional vibrational mode comprising 1 kinetic and 1 potential energy term: f = 7.

concept_notes.heading: Internal Energy and Specific Heats
bullets: The internal energy U of one mole of an ideal gas with f degrees of freedom is given by U = (f/2)RT.
Molar heat capacity at constant volume is C<sub>v</sub> = dU/dT = (f/2)R.
Molar heat capacity at constant pressure is C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>v</sub> + R = (f/2 + 1)R, leading to the adiabatic exponent γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub> = 1 + (2/f).

concept_notes.heading: Quantum Limitations and Vibrational Activation
bullets: At low temperatures, vibrational modes are 'frozen out' because the thermal energy k<sub>B</sub>T is much smaller than the quantum spacing between vibrational energy levels (ℏω).
As temperature increases, vibrational modes gradually get activated, increasing C<sub>v</sub> as predicted by quantum statistics rather than pure classical equipartition.
Classical equipartition overestimates specific heats at very low temperatures due to the neglect of quantum mechanical zero-point energy and discrete level spacing.

derivations.title: Derivation of Mean Energy per Degree of Freedom
derivations.conditions: System of particles obeying Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution in thermal equilibrium
steps: Consider a system whose total energy E contains a quadratic term corresponding to a specific degree of freedom, say E = ε + au<sup>2</sup>, where u is a velocity or coordinate component and a is a constant.

The average value of the quadratic term au<sup>2</sup> using the Boltzmann distribution is given by the statistical average ⟨au<sup>2</sup>⟩ = (∫ (au<sup>2</sup>) e<sup>-au<sup>2</sup>/k<sub>B</sub>T</sup> du) / (∫ e<sup>-au<sup>2</sup>/k<sub>B</sub>T</sup> du).
Evaluating the standard Gaussian integrals yields ⟨au<sup>2</sup>⟩ = (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T.
derivations.result: The average energy per quadratic term (degree of freedom) is (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T.

derivations.title: Derivation of Specific Heat Ratio (γ) from Degrees of Freedom
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas with f degrees of freedom
steps: Write the internal energy for n moles of gas: U = n(f/2)RT.
Differentiate with respect to temperature T at constant volume to obtain molar heat capacity: C<sub>v</sub> = (1/n)(dU/dT) = (f/2)R.
Use Mayer's relation C<sub>p</sub> - C<sub>v</sub> = R to find C<sub>p</sub> = (f/2 + 1)R.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of Molar Heat Capacity (C<sub>v</sub>) of Diatomic Gas with Temperature
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of C<sub>v</sub>/R versus Absolute Temperature T, showing steps at 5/2 (low T), 7/2 (intermediate T), and higher values due to dissociation at extreme temperatures.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates quantum freezing of rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom at low temperatures, refuting strict classical equipartition.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual PGT questions regarding failure of classical theory at cryogenic temperatures.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Energy Distribution Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Asymmetric bell-shaped curve plotting fraction of molecules versus kinetic energy, skewed towards higher energies.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that while individual molecular energies fluctuate widely, the mean energy per degree of freedom remains fixed at (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test the statistical basis of thermal energy distribution.

solved_numericals.question: Find the ratio of specific heats (γ) for a gas whose molecules are rigid diatomic.
solution_steps: Identify the degrees of freedom for a rigid diatomic molecule: f = 3 (translational) + 2 (rotational) = 5.
Substitute f into the adiabatic index formula: γ = 1 + (2/f).

solved_numericals.question: A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of oxygen (diatomic, rigid) and 4 moles of argon (monoatomic). Calculate the total internal energy of the mixture at temperature T.
solution_steps: Find internal energy of oxygen: U<sub>1</sub> = n<sub>1</sub>(f<sub>1</sub>/2)RT = 2 * (5/2)RT = 5RT.
Find internal energy of argon: U<sub>2</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>(f<sub>2</sub>/2)RT = 4 * (3/2)RT = 6RT.
Sum the internal energies: U<sub>total</sub> = U<sub>1</sub> + U<sub>2</sub> = 5RT + 6RT = 11RT.

solved_numericals.question: A triatomic gas molecule is non-linear and includes 1 vibrational mode active at high temperature. Calculate its molar heat capacity C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub>.
solution_steps: Determine degrees of freedom: Translational f<sub>trans</sub> = 3, Rotational f<sub>rot</sub> = 3. Non-linear triatomic total = 6.
Vibrational mode contributes 2 terms (kinetic and potential), so add 2 degrees of freedom: Total active f = 6 + 2 = 8.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes molecules are non-interacting point particles obeying classical mechanics, which fails at high pressures and low temperatures where intermolecular potentials become significant.
Fails to account for discrete quantum energy levels, incorrectly predicting constant specific heats down to absolute zero (Dulong-Petit anomaly in gases and solids).

common_misconceptions.wrong: All degrees of freedom are active at all temperatures.
common_misconceptions.correct: Vibrational and rotational degrees of freedom freeze out at low temperatures due to quantum spacing.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal energy k<sub>B</sub>T becomes smaller than the quantum excitation energy (ΔE) at cryogenic temperatures.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Internal energy depends only on translational kinetic energy for all gases.
common_misconceptions.correct: Internal energy includes contributions from rotational and vibrational modes depending on atomicity.
common_misconceptions.why: Polyatomic molecules can store energy in rotational and internal vibrational configurations.

quick_revision: Each quadratic term in energy contributes (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T per molecule or (1/2)RT per mole.
